Thanks for making the time. I read your one-pager this morning, but tell me in your own words: what does Invent actually do?
We build software that sits between a customer's ERP and everything else they use. In practice, we integrate with SAP, Oracle and the local systems.
And who buys it? Large corporations?
Mostly mid-market companies. Four people handle thousands of invoices a month there, and that is the use case we solve.
That is clearer than the one-pager, honestly. And you? What is your role there?
I am Head of Sales. I report to the CEO, and at the moment I am covering the international pipeline myself, while we hire a director.
So you are the person I should be talking to. Are you rolling out anything new this quarter?
We are rolling out a connector for a European ERP right now, and that is why I wanted this call. And you? How does your team usually choose the vendors you work with?
We integrate with SAP, Oracle and the local systems.

I stopped opening a first call with a sentence about the platform a long time ago. Nobody on the other side wants the technology in the first minute, and honestly they are not listening yet. So I open with their Monday morning instead. I say: somewhere in your company there is a person who spends Monday looking for an invoice that three different systems disagree about. That is the sentence that makes people put down their phone. Then I tell them who we sell to. Mid-market companies, always. Big enough to have a real problem, small enough that one person still knows everybody's name. And then, because a partner always wants to know what is moving right now and not only what we always do, I tell them what the team is working on this quarter. At the moment we are rolling out a new integration, and we are giving it to a small group of customers first, before anybody else touches it.

I take about six of these calls a week, and I will be honest with you: the decision is usually made in the first ten minutes. Not because I am in a hurry, but because the first ten minutes tell me everything. The vendors I call back describe a customer I recognise. They say something like, four people are handling thousands of invoices a month and nobody can close the month on time, and I think, yes, I know that company, I have three of them. The ones I do not call back describe a product. Beautiful architecture, very complete, fully configurable, and after five minutes I still cannot picture who is using it or why. One more thing, because people ask me this and they are usually embarrassed to. English that is not perfect has never been the reason I said no. Not once. What loses the call is a long answer with no customer in it.
